claim: Voltage-gated potassium channels (Kvs) are gated by transmembrane voltage sensors (VS) that move in response to changes in membrane voltage.
source: Voltage-gated potassium channels (Kvs) are gated by transmembrane voltage sensors (VS) that move in response to changes in membrane voltage.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about voltage-gated potassium channels.

claim: Kv10.1 (Eag1) has three intracellular domains: PAS, C-linker, and CNBHD.
source: Kv10.1 or Eag1 also has three intracellular domains: PAS, C-linker, and CNBHD.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Eag1 intracellular domains are not required for voltage-dependent gating.
source: We demonstrate that the Eag1 intracellular domains are not required for voltage-dependent gating but likely interact with the VS to modulate gating.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional data from the Eag1TM construct shown in Figure 2.

claim: The Eag1 intracellular domains interact with the VS to modulate gating.
source: We demonstrate that the Eag1 intracellular domains are not required for voltage-dependent gating but likely interact with the VS to modulate gating.
evidence: This is supported by functional data showing differences in gating kinetics between WT and mutant channels.

claim: Specific interactions between the PAS, CNBHD, and VS modulate voltage-dependent gating.
source: We identified specific interactions between the PAS, CNBHD, and VS that modulate voltage-dependent gating and provide evidence that VS movement destabilizes these interactions to promote channel opening.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis data and structural analysis presented in Figures 3-5.

claim: VS movement destabilizes interactions between PAS, CNBHD, and VS to promote channel opening.
source: We identified specific interactions between the PAS, CNBHD, and VS that modulate voltage-dependent gating and provide evidence that VS movement destabilizes these interactions to promote channel opening.
evidence: This is inferred from functional data on mutants and split channels.

claim: Mutation of interactions between PAS, CNBHD, and VS renders Eag1 insensitive to calmodulin inhibition.
source: Additionally, mutation of these interactions renders Eag1 insensitive to calmodulin inhibition.
evidence: This is demonstrated by functional data on the Δ3-13 mutant shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Channel opening may occur through a rotation of the intracellular domains.
source: The structure of the calmodulin insensitive mutant in a pre-open conformation suggests that channel opening may occur through a rotation of the intracellular domains and calmodulin may prevent this rotation by stabilizing interactions between the VS and intracellular domains.
evidence: This is based on structural data from the Eag1 Δ3-13/CaM structure shown in Figure 6.

claim: Calmodulin may prevent channel opening by stabilizing interactions between the VS and intracellular domains.
source: The structure of the calmodulin insensitive mutant in a pre-open conformation suggests that channel opening may occur through a rotation of the intracellular domains and calmodulin may prevent this rotation by stabilizing interactions between the VS and intracellular domains.
evidence: This is inferred from structural and functional data on CaM binding and inhibition.

claim: All Kvs are tetramers and consist of 6 transmembrane segments (S1-S6).
source: All Kvs are tetramers and consist of 6 transmembrane segments (S1-S6) (Jiang et al., 2003; Long et al., 2005a; Long et al., 2007; Sun and MacKinnon, 2017; Wang and MacKinnon, 2017; Whicher and MacKinnon, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: S1-S4 form the voltage sensor (VS) and S5-S6 form the potassium pore.
source: S1-S4 form the voltage sensor (VS) and S5-S6 form the potassium pore.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Kv channel architecture.

claim: The S4 helix of the VS is positively charged and was proposed to move within the membrane in response to changes in membrane voltage.
source: The S4 helix of the VS is positively charged and was proposed to move within the membrane in response to changes in membrane voltage (Aggarwal and MacKinnon, 1996; Seoh et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Upon membrane hyperpolarization the S4 was predicted to move 'down' towards the intracellular side of the membrane to close the potassium pore.
source: Upon membrane hyperpolarization the S4 was predicted to move 'down' towards in the intracellular side of the membrane to close the potassium pore and upon membrane depolarization the S4 was predicted to move 'up' to the extracellular side of the membrane to open the potassium pore.
evidence: This is a prediction based on established models of voltage-gated channel function.

claim: Upon membrane depolarization the S4 was predicted to move 'up' to the extracellular side of the membrane to open the potassium pore.
source: Upon membrane hyperpolarization the S4 was predicted to move 'down' towards in the intracellular side of the membrane to close the potassium pore and upon membrane depolarization the S4 was predicted to move 'up' to the extracellular side of the membrane to open the potassium pore.
evidence: This is a prediction based on established models of voltage-gated channel function.

claim: In Kvs 1–9 movement of S4 is coupled to the potassium pore by a ~15 residue, helical S4-S5 linker.
source: In Kvs 1–9 movement of S4 is coupled to the potassium pore by a ~ 15 residue, helical S4-S5 linker, which forms a domain-swapped linkage between S4 and S5 that positions it directly above the pore lining S6 helix (Long et al., 2005a; Long et al., 2007; Sun and MacKinnon, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The S4-S5 linker in Kvs 1-9 forms a domain-swapped linkage between S4 and S5 that positions it directly above the pore lining S6 helix.
source: In Kvs 1–9 movement of S4 is coupled to the potassium pore by a ~ 15 residue, helical S4-S5 linker, which forms a domain-swapped linkage between S4 and S5 that positions it directly above the pore lining S6 helix (Long et al., 2005a; Long et al., 2007; Sun and MacKinnon, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The S4-S5 linker was proposed to function as a mechanical lever to couple movement of the S4 to the S6 helices to open and close the pore.
source: In this position, the S4-S5 linker was proposed to function as a mechanical lever to couple movement of the S4 to the S6 helices to open and close the pore (Long et al., 2005b).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by citation.

claim: In Kvs 10–12 the S4-S5 linker is only six residues, which is not long enough to form the domain-swapped linkage observed in Kvs 1–9.
source: However, in Kvs 10–12 the S4-S5 linker is only six residues, which is not long enough to form the domain-swapped linkage observed in Kvs 1–9.
evidence: This is a structural observation based on sequence analysis.

claim: Recent structures of Eag1 (Kv10.1) and hErg (Kv11.1) revealed that the S4-S5 linker forms a non-domain swapped linkage between S4 and S5.
source: Indeed, recent structures of Eag1 (Kv10.1) and hErg (Kv11.1) revealed that the S4-S5 linker forms a non-domain swapped linkage between S4 and S5 and is unlikely to be domain swapped in any conformation (Figure 1a,b,c) (Wang and MacKinnon, 2017; Whicher and MacKinnon, 2016).
evidence: This is based on structural data from cited studies and Figure 1.

claim: The S4-S5 linker in Kvs 10-12 is unlikely to be domain swapped in any conformation.
source: Indeed, recent structures of Eag1 (Kv10.1) and hErg (Kv11.1) revealed that the S4-S5 linker forms a non-domain swapped linkage between S4 and S5 and is unlikely to be domain swapped in any conformation (Figure 1a,b,c) (Wang and MacKinnon, 2017; Whicher and MacKinnon, 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from structural data.

claim: Due to the non-domain swapped transmembrane architecture, the S4-S5 linker is not in the same position and does not appear to form a similar mechanical lever.
source: Due to the non-domain swapped transmembrane architecture, the S4-S5 linker is not in the same position and does not appear to form a similar mechanical lever, suggesting an alternative mechanism of voltage-dependent gating in Kvs 10–12 (Lörinczi et al., 2015; Tomczak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from structural observations and supported by citations.

claim: An alternative mechanism of voltage-dependent gating exists in Kvs 10–12.
source: Due to the non-domain swapped transmembrane architecture, the S4-S5 linker is not in the same position and does not appear to form a similar mechanical lever, suggesting an alternative mechanism of voltage-dependent gating in Kvs 10–12 (Lörinczi et al., 2015; Tomczak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from structural and functional data.

claim: The PAS domain is positioned directly below the VS.
source: For example, the PAS domain, which is positioned directly below the VS, has a 15-residue N-terminal loop (PAS loop) that is directed, through interactions with the VS and CNBHD, towards the S4-S5 linker (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is based on structural data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The PAS domain has a 15-residue N-terminal loop (PAS loop) that is directed, through interactions with the VS and CNBHD, towards the S4-S5 linker.
source: For example, the PAS domain, which is positioned directly below the VS, has a 15-residue N-terminal loop (PAS loop) that is directed, through interactions with the VS and CNBHD, towards the S4-S5 linker (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is based on structural data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The PAS loop has been implicated in voltage-dependent gating and the large Cole-Moore effect observed in Eag1.
source: The PAS loop has been implicated in voltage-dependent gating and the large Cole-Moore effect observed in Eag1, in which more hyperpolarized (negative) resting membrane potentials result in slower rates of activation (Cole and Moore, 1960; Ju and Wray, 2006; Ludwig et al., 1994; Terlau et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the Cole-Moore effect, more hyperpolarized (negative) resting membrane potentials result in slower rates of activation.
source: The PAS loop has been implicated in voltage-dependent gating and the large Cole-Moore effect observed in Eag1, in which more hyperpolarized (negative) resting membrane potentials result in slower rates of activation (Cole and Moore, 1960; Ju and Wray, 2006; Ludwig et al., 1994; Terlau et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a definition of the Cole-Moore effect supported by citations.

claim: The C-linker forms an intracellular ring directly below the S6 helices.
source: In addition, the C-linker forms an intracellular ring directly below the S6 helices, which are positioned to couple movements of the intracellular domains to the pore (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is based on structural data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The S6 helices are positioned to couple movements of the intracellular domains to the pore.
source: In addition, the C-linker forms an intracellular ring directly below the S6 helices, which are positioned to couple movements of the intracellular domains to the pore (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is inferred from structural data.

claim: The C-linker ring is near the S4-S5 linker and the S4, which adopts a depolarized or up conformation in the Eag1 structure.
source: The C-linker ring is near the S4-S5 linker and the S4, which adopts a depolarized or up conformation in the Eag1 structure (Whicher and MacKinnon, 2016).
evidence: This is based on structural data from a cited study.

claim: The S4 helix moves towards the intracellular side of the membrane during hyperpolarization to interact with and rotate the C-linker and S6 helices to close the potassium pore.
source: Since the S4-S5 linker of Eag1 appeared unlikely to function as a mechanical lever, we proposed a voltage-dependent gating mechanism in which the S4 helix moves towards the intracellular side of the membrane during hyperpolarization to interact with and rotate the C-linker and S6 helices to close the potassium pore (Whicher and MacKinnon, 2016).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on structural data.

claim: Eag1 is gated by the calcium sensor calmodulin (CaM).
source: In addition to voltage-dependent gating, Eag1 is also gated by the calcium sensor calmodulin (CaM) (Schönherr et al., 2000; Ziechner et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: CaM binds to Eag1 only in the presence of calcium and holds the pore closed even during membrane depolarization.
source: CaM binds to Eag1 only in the presence of calcium and holds the pore closed even during membrane depolarization.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CaM regulation of Eag1.

claim: Each PAS and CNBHD domain has a CaM binding site and thus there are eight binding sites per tetramer.
source: Each PAS and CNBHD domain has a CaM binding site and thus there are eight binding sites per tetramer.
evidence: This is based on structural and biochemical data.

claim: In the Eag1 structure, each CaM molecule occupies two binding sites, one on the PAS and one on the CNBHD, clamping the two domains together.
source: In the Eag1 structure, each CaM molecule occupies two binding sites, one on the PAS and one on the CNBHD, clamping the two domains together (Figure 1a) (Whicher and MacKinnon, 2016).
evidence: This is based on structural data from a cited study and Figure 1.

claim: The CaM binding orientation is essential for channel inhibition.
source: This binding orientation was shown to be essential for channel inhibition but it is unclear how CaM binding prevents opening of the pore.
evidence: This is based on previous functional studies.

claim: Eag1TM forms functional channels that are voltage dependent.
source: Eag1TM forms functional channels that are voltage dependent (Figure 2a,b), indicating that the intracellular domains are not essential for voltage-dependent gating and that an interaction between the S4 and C-linker is not required to close the potassium pore.
evidence: This is demonstrated by functional data shown in Figure 2.

claim: An interaction between the S4 and C-linker is not required to close the potassium pore.
source: Eag1TM forms functional channels that are voltage dependent (Figure 2a,b), indicating that the intracellular domains are not essential for voltage-dependent gating and that an interaction between the S4 and C-linker is not required to close the potassium pore.
evidence: This is inferred from functional data on Eag1TM.

claim: Eag1TM had a right shifted V0.5 of 46 mV compared to the WT Eag1 (19 mV).
source: Eag1TM had a right shifted V0.5 of 46 mV (zero-slope on the activation curve was not reached up to 100 mV and therefore an accurate value for V0.5 could not be measured) compared to the WT Eag1 (19 mV).
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The Eag1/hErg chimera has a V0.5 (2.5 mV) that is in between that of WT Eag1 and hErg (−22 mV).
source: In addition, the Eag1/hErg chimera has a V0.5 (2.5 mV) that is in between that of WT Eag1 and hErg (−22 mV) and exhibits slow rates of channel closure (deactivation), a characteristic of hErg channels.
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The Eag1/hErg chimera exhibits slow rates of channel closure (deactivation), a characteristic of hErg channels.
source: In addition, the Eag1/hErg chimera has a V0.5 (2.5 mV) that is in between that of WT Eag1 and hErg (−22 mV) and exhibits slow rates of channel closure (deactivation), a characteristic of hErg channels.
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Neither Eag1TM nor the Eag1/hErg chimera exhibits a Cole-Moore effect.
source: Neither mutant channel exhibits a Cole-Moore effect (Figure 2c), which, along with the slow deactivation of the Eag1/hErg chimera and the shifted V0.5 of both channels, demonstrates that the intracellular domains influence voltage-dependent gating kinetics.
evidence: This is demonstrated by functional data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The intracellular domains influence voltage-dependent gating kinetics.
source: Neither mutant channel exhibits a Cole-Moore effect (Figure 2c), which, along with the slow deactivation of the Eag1/hErg chimera and the shifted V0.5 of both channels, demonstrates that the intracellular domains influence voltage-dependent gating kinetics.
evidence: This is inferred from functional data on multiple mutants.

claim: The Cole-Moore effect may arise from an interaction between the transmembrane and intracellular domains.
source: In addition, this result suggests that the Cole-Moore effect may arise from an interaction between the transmembrane and intracellular domains.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of Cole-Moore effect in mutants lacking intracellular domains.

claim: Mutation of Asp 342 to Ala (D342A) results in complete loss of the Cole-Moore effect.
source: We note that only mutation of Asp 342 to Ala (D342A) results in complete loss of the Cole-Moore effect, suggesting that Asp 342 may interact with the intracellular domains (Figure 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by functional data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Asp 342 may interact with the intracellular domains.
source: We note that only mutation of Asp 342 to Ala (D342A) results in complete loss of the Cole-Moore effect, suggesting that Asp 342 may interact with the intracellular domains (Figure 3).
evidence: This is inferred from functional data on the D342A mutant.

claim: Asp 342 is located at the C-terminus of S4 and is highly conserved in Kvs 10–12.
source: Asp 342 is located at the C-terminus of S4 and is highly conserved in Kvs 10–12.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and structural data.

claim: In the closed conformation of Eag1, Asp 342 does not interact with the intracellular domains.
source: In the closed conformation of Eag1, Asp 342 does not interact with the intracellular domains (Figure 1b) (Whicher and MacKinnon, 2016).
evidence: This is based on structural data from a cited study and Figure 1.

claim: In the open conformation of hErg the homologous Asp is near (~6 Å) two Arg residues in the PAS loop.
source: However, in the open conformation of hErg the homologous Asp is near (~6 Å) two Arg residues in the PAS loop (Figure 1c) (Wang and MacKinnon, 2017).
evidence: This is based on structural data from a cited study and Figure 1.

claim: In all Kvs 10–12 the PAS loop has at least one positively charged residue.
source: In all Kvs 10–12 the PAS loop has at least one positively charged residue.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: In Eag1, the corresponding Arg residues are Arg 7 and 8.
source: In Eag1, the corresponding Arg residues are Arg 7 and 8.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and structural comparison.

claim: The V0.5 of R7A/R8A and Δ3–9 are right shifted to a similar extent as Eag1TM and the D342A mutant.
source: The V0.5 of R7A/R8A and Δ3–9 are right shifted to a similar extent as Eag1TM and the D342A mutant.
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Arg 7 and 8 promote channel opening.
source: Therefore, Arg 7 and 8 promote channel opening, like Asp 342, and mutation of these residues has a similar effect on V0.5 as loss of the intracellular domains.
evidence: This is inferred from functional data on R7A/R8A and Δ3-9 mutants.

claim: Mutation of Arg 7 and 8 has a similar effect on V0.5 as loss of the intracellular domains.
source: Therefore, Arg 7 and 8 promote channel opening, like Asp 342, and mutation of these residues has a similar effect on V0.5 as loss of the intracellular domains.
evidence: This is based on functional data comparing mutants.

claim: The R7A/R8A and Δ3–9 mutations result in a right-shifted V0.5CM.
source: In addition, the R7A/R8A and Δ3–9 mutations result in a right-shifted V0.5CM, indicating that more depolarized holding potentials are required for fast activation of these mutants than WT Eag1.
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 3.

claim: More depolarized holding potentials are required for fast activation of R7A/R8A and Δ3-9 mutants than WT Eag1.
source: In addition, the R7A/R8A and Δ3–9 mutations result in a right-shifted V0.5CM, indicating that more depolarized holding potentials are required for fast activation of these mutants than WT Eag1.
evidence: This is inferred from the right-shifted V0.5CM values.

claim: Arg 7 and 8 might form a functional interaction with Asp 342.
source: The right shifted V0.5 and the modified Cole-Moore effect of R7A/R8A and Δ3–9 suggest that Arg 7 and 8 might form a functional interaction with Asp 342.
evidence: This is inferred from functional data on mutants.

claim: Asp 342 likely interacts with additional residues on the intracellular domains beyond Arg 7 and 8.
source: Furthermore, since mutation of Arg 7 and 8 did not result in complete loss of the Cole-Moore effect, Asp 342 likely interacts with additional residues on the intracellular domains.
evidence: This is inferred from the incomplete loss of Cole-Moore effect in R7A/R8A mutant.

claim: An interaction between Asp 342 and the PAS loop may occur in the open conformation to promote channel opening.
source: Taken together, the functional data along with the proximity of the PAS loop and Asp 342 in the open conformation of hErg suggest that an interaction between Asp 342 and the PAS loop may occur in the open conformation to promote channel opening.
evidence: This is inferred from functional and structural data.

claim: Leu 10, Val 11, Ala 12, and Pro 13 interact with Tyr 639 and Tyr 213.
source: Leu 10, Val 11, Ala 12, and Pro 13 interact with Tyr 639, a conserved residue in Kvs 10–12 that is located on the CNBHD, and Tyr 213, a Phe, Tyr or Cys in Kvs 10–12 that is located on the loop before S1 of the VS (Figure 1b) (Whicher and MacKinnon, 2016).
evidence: This is based on structural data from a cited study and Figure 1.

claim: Tyr 639 is a conserved residue in Kvs 10–12 that is located on the CNBHD.
source: Leu 10, Val 11, Ala 12, and Pro 13 interact with Tyr 639, a conserved residue in Kvs 10–12 that is located on the CNBHD, and Tyr 213, a Phe, Tyr or Cys in Kvs 10–12 that is located on the loop before S1 of the VS (Figure 1b) (Whicher and MacKinnon, 2016).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and structural data.

claim: Tyr 213 is a Phe, Tyr or Cys in Kvs 10–12 that is located on the loop before S1 of the VS.
source: Leu 10, Val 11, Ala 12, and Pro 13 interact with Tyr 639, a conserved residue in Kvs 10–12 that is located on the CNBHD, and Tyr 213, a Phe, Tyr or Cys in Kvs 10–12 that is located on the loop before S1 of the VS (Figure 1b) (Whicher and MacKinnon, 2016).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and structural data.

claim: Residues 10–13 link the VS and the intracellular CNBHD.
source: In this position, residues 10–13 link the VS and the intracellular CNBHD.
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: Y213A, Y639R, and PAS loop mutants with successive deletions of residues 10–13 show inactivation and hooked tail currents at more depolarized potentials (40–100 mV).
source: These mutants show inactivation and hooked tail currents at more depolarized potentials (40–100 mV), as was previously shown (Terlau et al., 1997) (Figure 4a,b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 4 and cited studies.

claim: Y213A, Y639R, and PAS loop deletion mutants produce channels that open at more negative (hyperpolarized) potentials than WT Eag1 (−80 mV).
source: These mutants also produce channels that open at more negative (hyperpolarized) potentials than WT Eag1 (−80 mV) and exhibit slow deactivation, demonstrating that the interaction between residues 10–13, Tyr 213, and Tyr 639 promotes the closed state of Eag1.
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Y213A, Y639R, and PAS loop deletion mutants exhibit slow deactivation.
source: These mutants also produce channels that open at more negative (hyperpolarized) potentials than WT Eag1 (−80 mV) and exhibit slow deactivation, demonstrating that the interaction between residues 10–13, Tyr 213, and Tyr 639 promotes the closed state of Eag1.
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The interaction between residues 10–13, Tyr 213, and Tyr 639 promotes the closed state of Eag1.
source: These mutants also produce channels that open at more negative (hyperpolarized) potentials than WT Eag1 (−80 mV) and exhibit slow deactivation, demonstrating that the interaction between residues 10–13, Tyr 213, and Tyr 639 promotes the closed state of Eag1.
evidence: This is inferred from functional data on mutants.

claim: The PAS loop can be divided into two functionally distinct segments: the N-terminus (residues 1–9) and the C-terminus (residues 10–13).
source: Based on these data, the PAS loop can be divided into two functionally distinct segments: the N-terminus (residues 1–9; not observed in the Eag1 structure) and the C-terminus (residues 10–13) (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is inferred from functional data on different PAS loop mutants.

claim: The PAS loop N-terminus (residues 1-9) seems to promote channel opening and may interact with Asp 342 of the S4-S5 linker.
source: The N-terminus seems to promote channel opening and may interact with Asp 342 of the S4-S5 linker.
evidence: This is inferred from functional data on mutants.

claim: The PAS loop C-terminus (residues 10-13) seems to promote channel closure and interacts with the CNBHD.
source: The C-terminus seems to promote channel closure and interacts with the CNBHD.
evidence: This is inferred from functional data on mutants.

claim: In the open state structure of hErg the PAS loop C-terminus does not interact with either Tyr 403 or Tyr 827.
source: Furthermore, in the open state structure of hErg the PAS loop C-terminus does not interact with either Tyr 403 (equivalent to Tyr 213 in Eag1) or Tyr 827 (equivalent to Tyr 639 in Eag1) (Figure 1c) suggesting that destabilization of this interface might be necessary for channel opening (Wang and MacKinnon, 2017).
evidence: This is based on structural data from a cited study and Figure 1.

claim: Destabilization of the interface between PAS loop C-terminus, Tyr 213, and Tyr 639 might be necessary for channel opening.
source: Furthermore, in the open state structure of hErg the PAS loop C-terminus does not interact with either Tyr 403 (equivalent to Tyr 213 in Eag1) or Tyr 827 (equivalent to Tyr 639 in Eag1) (Figure 1c) suggesting that destabilization of this interface might be necessary for channel opening (Wang and MacKinnon, 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from structural data.

claim: Upon depolarization, Asp 342 interacts with the PAS loop N-terminus to stabilize the open state of the VS and destabilize the interaction between the PAS loop C-terminus, Tyr 213, and Tyr 639 to promote channel opening.
source: Therefore, we propose that the following structural interactions take place in association with voltage dependent gating. Upon depolarization, Asp 342 interacts with the PAS loop N-terminus to stabilize the open state of the VS and destabilize the interaction between the PAS loop C-terminus, Tyr 213, and Tyr 639 to promote channel opening (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on functional and structural data.

claim: When the VS is hyperpolarized, movement of the S4 disrupts the interaction between Asp 342 and the PAS loop N-terminus, allowing the interaction between the PAS loop C-terminus, Tyr 213, and Tyr 639 to form and promote channel closing.
source: When the VS is hyperpolarized, movement of the S4 disrupts the interaction between Asp 342 and the PAS loop N-terminus, allowing the interaction between the PAS loop C-terminus, Tyr 213, and Tyr 639 to form and promote channel closing (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on functional and structural data.

claim: Co-expression of two halves of a split Eag1 construct (L341 split) produces a partially constitutively open channel.
source: First, co-expression of two halves of a split Eag1 construct (L341 split), in which the N-terminal half of the channel includes Met 1-Leu 341 and the C-terminal half includes Asp 342-Ser 962, produces a partially constitutively open channel (Figure 5a) (Tomczak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 5 and cited studies.

claim: In the split Eag1 construct Asp 342 is no longer connected to S4 of the VS and thus is no longer forced to move when the VS moves.
source: This functional behavior can be explained by the above hypothesis because in the split Eag1 construct Asp 342 is no longer connected to S4 of the VS and thus is no longer forced to move when the VS moves.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the split construct.

claim: Asp 342 can maintain its interaction with the PAS loop to promote channel opening in the split construct.
source: Consequently, Asp 342 can maintain its interaction with the PAS loop to promote channel opening.
evidence: This is inferred from the constitutively open phenotype of the split channel.

claim: Introduction of the D342A and Δ3–9 mutations into the Eag1 split construct produce channels that close at hyperpolarized potentials.
source: In agreement with this conclusion, introduction of the D342A and Δ3–9 mutations into the Eag1 split construct produce channels that close at hyperpolarized potentials (Figure 5b,c) (Tomczak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 5 and cited studies.

claim: The Cole-Moore effect was proposed to be due to the existence of multiple closed states that the VS must transition through in order to reach an active or depolarized conformation.
source: Second, this mechanism provides an explanation for the Cole-Moore effect. The Cole-Moore effect was proposed to be due to the existence of multiple closed states that the VS must transition through in order to reach an active or depolarized conformation (Cole and Moore, 1960).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by citation.

claim: At more negative holding potentials the VS might have to transition through more closed states in order for the S4 and Asp 342 to interact with the PAS loop N-terminus, which will result in slower activation times.
source: In Eag, at more negative holding potentials the VS might have to transition through more closed states in order for the S4 and Asp 342 to interact with the PAS loop N-terminus, which will result in slower activation times.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism to explain the Cole-Moore effect in Eag1.

claim: If we remove the interaction between the PAS loop C-terminus, Tyr 213, and Tyr 639, then the Cole-Moore effect should be lost.
source: Therefore, if we remove the interaction between the PAS loop C-terminus, Tyr 213, and Tyr 639, which we propose is destabilized when Asp 342 interacts with the PAS loop N-terminus, then the Cole-Moore effect should be lost.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: Δ3–12 and Δ3–13 do not exhibit a Cole-Moore effect.
source: In agreement with this line of reasoning, Δ3–12 and Δ3–13 do not exhibit a Cole-Moore effect while Y213A, Y639R, Δ3–10, and Δ3–11 show a reduced Cole-Moore effect compared to the WT channel (Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Y213A, Y639R, Δ3–10, and Δ3–11 show a reduced Cole-Moore effect compared to the WT channel.
source: In agreement with this line of reasoning, Δ3–12 and Δ3–13 do not exhibit a Cole-Moore effect while Y213A, Y639R, Δ3–10, and Δ3–11 show a reduced Cole-Moore effect compared to the WT channel (Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the presence of Ca2+/CaM, Eag1 Δ3–13 remains open at hyperpolarized voltages.
source: In the presence of Ca2+/CaM, Eag1 Δ3–13 remains open at hyperpolarized voltages (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Two different conformations were identified for Eag1 Δ3–13/CaM: conformation 1 at 3.7 Å and conformation 2 at 4.0 Å resolution.
source: Two different conformations were identified for Eag1 Δ3–13/CaM: conformation 1 at 3.7 Å and conformation 2 at 4.0 Å resolution.
evidence: This is based on Cryo-EM structure determination.

claim: In both conformations of Eag1 Δ3-13/CaM, the S4 helices adopt a depolarized conformation.
source: In both conformations, the S4 helices adopt a depolarized conformation and intracellular domains are rotated in a counterclockwise direction when viewed from the extracellular side of the membrane, but in conformation two the extent of the rotation is larger (2.4° degrees for conformation 1 and 8.6° degrees for conformation 2) (Figure 6b,c and Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on structural data shown in Figure 6.

claim: In both conformations of Eag1 Δ3-13/CaM, intracellular domains are rotated in a counterclockwise direction when viewed from the extracellular side of the membrane.
source: In both conformations, the S4 helices adopt a depolarized conformation and intracellular domains are rotated in a counterclockwise direction when viewed from the extracellular side of the membrane, but in conformation two the extent of the rotation is larger (2.4° degrees for conformation 1 and 8.6° degrees for conformation 2) (Figure 6b,c and Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on structural data shown in Figure 6.

claim: In conformation 1 of Eag1 Δ3-13/CaM the rotation is 2.4 degrees.
source: In both conformations, the S4 helices adopt a depolarized conformation and intracellular domains are rotated in a counterclockwise direction when viewed from the extracellular side of the membrane, but in conformation two the extent of the rotation is larger (2.4° degrees for conformation 1 and 8.6° degrees for conformation 2) (Figure 6b,c and Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on structural data shown in Figure 6.

claim: In conformation 2 of Eag1 Δ3-13/CaM the rotation is 8.6 degrees.
source: In both conformations, the S4 helices adopt a depolarized conformation and intracellular domains are rotated in a counterclockwise direction when viewed from the extracellular side of the membrane, but in conformation two the extent of the rotation is larger (2.4° degrees for conformation 1 and 8.6° degrees for conformation 2) (Figure 6b,c and Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on structural data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The rotation observed in Eag1 Δ3-13/CaM conformations is in a similar direction as the intracellular domains in the open conformation structure of hErg.
source: The rotation observed in these conformations is in a similar direction as the intracellular domains in the open conformation structure of hErg (Wang and MacKinnon, 2017) (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 6d.

claim: The extent of the rotation of the Eag1 intracellular domains is not as large as the 20° rotation observed in hErg.
source: However, the extent of the rotation of the Eag1 intracellular domains is not as large as the 20° rotation observed in hErg and the S6 helices remain closed (Figure 6d,e).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 6.

claim: The S6 helices remain closed in the Eag1 Δ3-13/CaM structures.
source: However, the extent of the rotation of the Eag1 intracellular domains is not as large as the 20° rotation observed in hErg and the S6 helices remain closed (Figure 6d,e).
evidence: This is based on structural data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Conformation 1 and conformation 2 of Eag1 Δ3-13/CaM represent pre-open conformations of Eag1 on the pathway from closed to fully open.
source: As a result, we believe that conformation 1 and conformation 2 represent pre-open conformations of Eag1 on the pathway from closed to fully open.
evidence: This is inferred from structural data showing partial rotation with closed pore.

claim: Eag1 might be more stable in a closed conformation compared to hErg.
source: A hypothesis for why the pore remains closed in the structure of Eag1 Δ3–13/CaM is that, compared to hErg, Eag1 might be more stable in a closed conformation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the structural observations.

claim: Insertion of the intracellular domains of hErg onto Eag1 (Eag1/hErg chimera) causes a 20 mV left shift in the V0.5.
source: First, insertion of the intracellular domains of hErg onto Eag1 (Eag1/hErg chimera) causes a 20 mV left shift in the V0.5 (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The V0.5 of Eag1 is right-shifted by 40 mV compared with hErg.
source: Second, the V0.5 of Eag1 is right-shifted by 40 mV compared with hErg and Eag1TM is right shifted by 80 mV when compared to a hErg channel lacking the intracellular domains (Figure 2a,b) (Hausammann and Grütter, 2013; Wang and MacKinnon, 2017).
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 2 and cited studies.

claim: Eag1TM is right shifted by 80 mV when compared to a hErg channel lacking the intracellular domains.
source: Second, the V0.5 of Eag1 is right-shifted by 40 mV compared with hErg and Eag1TM is right shifted by 80 mV when compared to a hErg channel lacking the intracellular domains (Figure 2a,b) (Hausammann and Grütter, 2013; Wang and MacKinnon, 2017).
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 2 and cited studies.

claim: In Eag1, Phe 475 and Gln 477 are located at the interface of the S6 helices on either side of Gln 476, the intracellular gate.
source: In Eag1, Phe 475 and Gln 477 are located at the interface of the S6 helices on either side of Gln 476, the intracellular gate.
evidence: This is based on structural data.

claim: In Kv11 and Kv12, which have a left shifted V0.5 compared to Eag1, the residues corresponding to Phe 475 and Gln 477 are Ile and Arg respectively.
source: In Kv11 and Kv12, which have a left shifted V0.5 compared to Eag1, these residues are Ile and Arg respectively (Bauer and Schwarz, 2018).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and cited studies.

claim: The Eag1 double mutant F475I/Q477R causes a 50 mV left shift in the V0.5 to −20 mV when introduced into the full-length channel.
source: The Eag1 double mutant F475I/Q477R causes a 50 mV left shift in the V0.5 to −20 mV when introduced into the full-length channel and a 16 mV left shift in the V0.5 to 30 mV when introduced into Eag1TM (Figure 7a,b,c).
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The F475I/Q477R mutation causes a 16 mV left shift in the V0.5 to 30 mV when introduced into Eag1TM.
source: The Eag1 double mutant F475I/Q477R causes a 50 mV left shift in the V0.5 to −20 mV when introduced into the full-length channel and a 16 mV left shift in the V0.5 to 30 mV when introduced into Eag1TM (Figure 7a,b,c).
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 7.

claim: When the F475I/Q477R mutation is introduced into the Eag1/hErg chimera the channel remains open at hyperpolarized potentials.
source: In addition, when the F475I/Q477R mutation is introduced into the Eag1/hErg chimera the channel remains open at hyperpolarized potentials (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: The intracellular domains and Phe 475 and Gln 477 cause Eag1 to be more stable in a closed conformation.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the intracellular domains and Phe 475 and Gln 477 cause Eag1 to be more stable in a closed conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from functional data on mutants.

claim: The Eag1 intracellular domains, when viewed from the extracellular side, rotate in a counterclockwise direction to promote the opening of the pore.
source: Therefore, we propose that the Eag1 intracellular domains, when viewed from the extracellular side, rotate in a counterclockwise direction to promote the opening of the pore.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on structural data.

claim: Due to the stability of Eag1 in a closed conformation and the conditions under which the Cryo-EM structure was determined, pore opening is transient and thus not observed in the Eag1 Δ3–13/CaM structure.
source: However, due to the stability of Eag1 in a closed conformation and the conditions under which the Cryo-EM structure was determined we suspect that pore opening is transient and thus not observed in the Eag1 Δ3–13/CaM structure.
evidence: This is an explanation for why the pore remains closed in the structure.

claim: Rotation of the intracellular domains observed in the different conformations of Eag1 Δ3–13/CaM occurs with CaM bound to the channel in the same orientation as observed in the WT structure.
source: Rotation of the intracellular domains observed in the different conformations of Eag1 Δ3–13/CaM occurs with CaM bound to the channel in the same orientation as observed in the WT structure (Figure 6—figure supplement 4) (Whicher and MacKinnon, 2016).
evidence: This is based on structural data shown in Figure 6 supplement 4.

claim: Binding of CaM does not clamp the PAS and CNBHD domains together to prevent rotation of the intracellular domains and channel opening.
source: This finding suggests that binding of CaM does not clamp the PAS and CNBHD domains together to prevent rotation of the intracellular domains and channel opening as we previously proposed.
evidence: This is inferred from structural data showing rotation with CaM bound.

claim: CaM binding to the channel helps to stabilize the hydrophobic interaction between the PAS loop C-terminus, Tyr 213, and Tyr 639.
source: Instead, we think that more likely CaM binding to the channel helps to stabilize the hydrophobic interaction between the PAS loop C-terminus, Tyr 213, and Tyr 639.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism for CaM inhibition.

claim: By stabilizing the interaction between PAS loop C-terminus, Tyr 213, and Tyr 639, CaM can inhibit the channel.
source: As discussed above, this interaction seems to be important for channel closure. Thus, by stabilizing this interaction CaM can inhibit the channel.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism for CaM inhibition.

claim: Deletion of the interaction between PAS loop C-terminus, Tyr 213, and Tyr 639 by removing residues 3–13 results in a channel that is no longer inhibited by CaM.
source: In support of this hypothesis, deletion of this interaction by removing residues 3–13 results in a channel that is no longer inhibited by CaM (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is based on functional data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: A similar effect to Δ3-13 was observed in Eag1 mutants that lack the PAS cap (residues 1–26) or the entire PAS domain (27-135).
source: In addition, a similar effect was observed in Eag1 mutants that lack the PAS cap (residues 1–26) or the entire PAS domain (27-135) (Lörinczi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on cited studies.

claim: Intracellular domains likely play a similar modulatory role in voltage-dependent gating of the related Kv11-12 channels.
source: Intracellular domains likely play a similar modulatory role in voltage-dependent gating of the related Kv11-12 channels.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of Kv10-12 channels.

claim: In hErg deletion of the intracellular domains and mutation of Asp 540 does not change the V0.5.
source: However, in hErg deletion of the intracellular domains and mutation of Asp 540 does not change the V0.5, suggesting that the interaction between the PAS N-terminus and Asp 540 is not important for channel activation (Hausammann and Grütter, 2013; Morais Cabral et al., 1998; Sanguinetti and Xu, 1999).
evidence: This is based on cited studies.

claim: The interaction between the PAS N-terminus and Asp 540 is not important for channel activation in hErg.
source: However, in hErg deletion of the intracellular domains and mutation of Asp 540 does not change the V0.5, suggesting that the interaction between the PAS N-terminus and Asp 540 is not important for channel activation (Hausammann and Grütter, 2013; Morais Cabral et al., 1998; Sanguinetti and Xu, 1999).
evidence: This is inferred from functional data in cited studies.

claim: In hErg, the interaction between Asp 540 and the PAS loop forms after channel activation and prevents pore closing, which results in slow deactivation.
source: Instead, we propose that in hErg, which we have shown apparently has a more stable open conformation than Eag1, the interaction between Asp 540 and the PAS loop forms after channel activation and prevents pore closing, which results in slow deactivation.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism for hErg slow deactivation.

claim: The interaction between Asp 540 and the PAS loop N-terminus in hErg may prevent pore closing by destabilizing the interaction between the PAS loop C-terminus, Tyr 403, and Tyr 827.
source: Like Eag1, the interaction between Asp 540 and the PAS loop N-terminus in hErg may prevent pore closing by destabilizing the interaction between the PAS loop C-terminus, Tyr 403, and Tyr 827.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on analogy to Eag1.

claim: Splitting the hErg channel so that Asp 540 is not covalently linked to the voltage sensor produces a channel that displays slowed deactivation compared to WT hErg.
source: In support of this idea, splitting the hErg channel, analogous to the Eag1 L341 split, so that Asp 540 is not covalently linked to the voltage sensor, produces a channel that displays slowed deactivation compared to WT hErg (de la Peña et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on cited studies.

claim: CaM may be able to stabilize the PAS loop in a closed conformation by binding to the PAS domain.
source: Perhaps by binding to the PAS domain, CaM may be able to stabilize the PAS loop in a closed conformation.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism for CaM inhibition.

claim: Channel opening may occur through a counterclockwise rotation of the intracellular domains.
source: The structure of Eag1 Δ3–13/CaM in a pre-open conformation suggests that channel opening may occur through a counterclockwise rotation of the intracellular domains and channel closing may occur through a clockwise rotation of the intracellular domains.
evidence: This is inferred from structural data.

claim: Channel closing may occur through a clockwise rotation of the intracellular domains.
source: The structure of Eag1 Δ3–13/CaM in a pre-open conformation suggests that channel opening may occur through a counterclockwise rotation of the intracellular domains and channel closing may occur through a clockwise rotation of the intracellular domains.
evidence: This is inferred from structural data.

claim: CaM seems to function by stabilizing the interaction between residues 10–13, Tyr 213, and Tyr 639 to prevent pore opening.
source: Furthermore, CaM seems to function through this proposed mechanism by stabilizing the interaction between residues 10–13, Tyr 213, and Tyr 639 to prevent pore opening.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism for CaM inhibition.
